claims.text: The initial eutectic high-entropy alloy has dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries.
Internal boundaries in the lamellar colonies act as microcrack-nucleation sites.
A controlled annealing treatment, potentially preceded by light deformation, can improve both yield strength and room-temperature tensile ductility.
The proposed treatment can refine the lamellar-colony microstructure.
The proposed treatment can reduce detrimental internal stress concentrations.
Controlled annealing can slightly coarsen or reconfigure the lamellar spacing.
Controlled annealing can improve interphase-boundary characteristics.
Rapid cooling after annealing can retain a refined microstructure.
A suitable time-temperature window can promote stress relaxation and interfacial adjustment without excessive coarsening or deleterious phase changes.
Modified lamellar spacing and internal-boundary structures can reduce microcrack-initiation sites.
Relieving internal stresses and changing lamellar-boundary morphology decreases susceptibility to microcracking.
The proposed boundary and stress modifications can maintain or enhance the load-bearing capacity of the constituent phases.
Light deformation before annealing promotes a more homogeneous microstructure.
Rapid cooling locks in the microstructural features produced by the treatment.
The treated alloy will have higher yield strength than the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline.
The treated alloy will have greater room-temperature tensile ductility than the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline.
The conventionally processed baseline typically has high strength but limited ductility because microcracks initiate at internal boundaries.
Excessive grain coarsening or over-annealing may reduce strength.
Treatment efficacy depends on alloy composition, phase distribution, and the selected time-temperature regime.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says the treatment will refine the lamellar-colony microstructure, whereas the intervention is described as deliberately slightly coarsening or reconfiguring the lamellar spacing. The intended direction of the spacing change is therefore internally ambiguous.
The annealing step is allowed to coarsen the lamellae, but rapid cooling is said to retain or lock in a refined microstructure; the hypothesis does not explain how these descriptions are reconciled.
